overview: The Yuezhi story crosses a continent. Chinese histories place them near Dunhuang and Gansu, where Xiongnu victories in 176 and 162 BCE drove the greater group west. After another displacement near the Ili valley, they crossed Central Asia and became overlords of Bactria by about 130 BCE. There they met walled towns, farmers, merchants and Greek-style coins; migration did not turn every resident into Yuezhi. Zhang Qian found their royal camp north of the Oxus and reported that they declined a Han alliance. Later sources describe five regional chiefs. In the first century CE, Kushan chief Kujula Kadphises brought those domains together and began a much larger empire. The atlas gets this journey badly out of step: its only Yuezhi polygon, from 200 to 100 BCE, still covers Dunhuang and the Hexi corridor, then paints an enormous Kushan realm too early. Read those shapes as rough locators. The clearest material evidence comes later, from Khalchayan art, coins, inscriptions and successor cities, while Yuezhi language, ordinary schooling, medicine and toilets remain poorly documented.

periods.title: An atlas shape before the recorded defeats
periods.summary: The atlas already paints a Yuezhi region across Gansu and far westward. Historical narratives still place the powerful Yuezhi near Gansu before Maodun’s attack, so the polygon is a rough retrospective label rather than a dated frontier.

periods.title: Defeat and the first westward displacement
periods.summary: Iranica dates Maodun’s crushing defeat of the Yuezhi in Gansu to 176 BCE. Chinese accounts make this the beginning of forced movement, although they preserve political drama more clearly than the routes taken by ordinary households.

periods.title: Across western Central Asia
periods.summary: After the defeats, the greater Yuezhi moved beyond Ferghana toward Sogdiana and Bactria. Chinese histories also remembered a smaller group closer to the old homeland, so the migration did not carry every community along one route.

periods.title: Conquest north of the Oxus and entry into Bactria
periods.summary: Coin hoards and Chinese testimony support a staged takeover: nomadic groups first gained areas north of the Oxus, then Greco-Bactrian rule north of the Hindu Kush ended by roughly 130 BCE.

periods.title: Zhang Qian meets the Great Yuezhi
periods.summary: Zhang Qian reported a mobile Yuezhi royal court north of the Oxus and Bactrian cities subject to it. The court preferred its new rich country to renewed war against the Xiongnu and declined Han’s proposed alliance.

periods.title: Five chiefs, not the atlas’s instant empire
periods.summary: Later Chinese history describes five Yuezhi xihou, or regional chiefs, in Bactria. The atlas instead jumps to a vast Kushan Empire at 100 BCE and removes it at 1 BCE, neither of which supplies a secure historical transition.

periods.title: The Kushan branch rises
periods.summary: During the first century CE, Kujula Kadphises of the Kushan branch overcame the other Yuezhi chiefs and adopted royal titles. Exact years remain debated, but this consolidation happened long after the atlas’s 100 BCE handoff.

sections.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass

items.text: The exact atlas target is id “yuezhi,” labeled Yuezhi and indexed circa 200 to 100 BCE. Its only feature is one Polygon with one ring and 26 coordinate positions. The decoded bounds run from about 72.280° to 106.044° east and 30.175° to 48.408° north.

Point tests make the mismatch easy to see. Dunhuang and a central Hexi corridor point fall inside the 200 BCE shape, but the Ili valley, Issyk-Kul, Kashgar, Ferghana, Samarkand, Balkh, Termez, Kabul and Merv all fall outside. Geometry precision does not rescue historical timing.

At 100 BCE the atlas replaces Yuezhi with a huge Kushan polygon covering tested places from Kashgar to Merv and Kabul. At 1 BCE Kushan disappears, then a smaller Kushan feature returns in 100 CE. That flicker is a dataset seam, not two documented imperial collapses.

There is no yuezhi feature in the 300 BCE snapshot and no exact feature after 200 BCE. Appearance and disappearance therefore say only how this imported atlas grouped its snapshots. They do not date the people’s origin, migration, conquest of Bactria or transformation into Kushan rule.

Older scholarship often equated the Yuezhi with the Tocharians, but archaeology and language do not make that identity automatic. No surviving Yuezhi sentence tells us what language the migrating confederation spoke. Genetic labels, later manuscripts and similar names cannot be snapped together like puzzle pieces without evidence.

sections.title: A migration forced by rival powers

items.text: In 176 BCE, Xiongnu ruler Maodun defeated the Yuezhi in Gansu. This is a political and military event preserved by outside historians, not a census of every Yuezhi family. Some people moved, some may have followed later, and movement across such distances cannot be reduced to one arrow on a map.

Around 162 BCE, Laoshang again crushed Yuezhi refugees in the Ili valley and pushed the greater group southwest. The two dated defeats explain why the journey came in stages. They also show why the atlas’s single 200 BCE shape cannot represent one stable homeland or surveyed state.

The Shiji says a smaller group unable to follow took refuge among Qiang communities near the southern mountains and became known as the Little Yuezhi. “Great” and “Little” are labels in Chinese records. They should not be turned into neat, biologically separate peoples.

Chapter 123 of the Shiji centers on Zhang Qian’s mission to the Dayuezhi. A rare-book witness preserved by Toyo Bunko now has page images and DOI metadata online. The archive notes that his observations informed later Han action and that a second western mission followed in 116 BCE.

Zhang Qian found that the Yuezhi had conquered fertile Bactria and no longer wanted revenge badly enough to march east for Han. Their refusal shows political choice after catastrophe: leaders weighed distance, safety and new resources rather than obediently following the alliance plan imagined in Chang’an.

Greek and Roman writers name several nomadic groups in Bactria, while Chinese histories foreground the Yuezhi. Saka studies warn that pottery and invasions cannot always be assigned to one ethnicity. The end of Greco-Bactrian rule was a tangled regional change, not a clean handover between two uniform nations.

Around 130 BCE, Zhang Qian described Yuezhi camping grounds north of the Oxus and many Bactrian city principalities south of it under Yuezhi domination. Mobile rulers and settled subjects could exist together. Calling the whole population “Yuezhi” would erase Bactrian farmers, traders and local chiefs.

The Hou Han Shu later names five xihou or yabghus: Xiumi, Shuangmi, Guishuang, Xidun and Dumi. Scholars debate the places behind those transcriptions. What matters for this card is the political structure: several regional chiefs shared the Yuezhi-Bactrian world before one Kushan branch became dominant.

Coin hoards from Kunduz and Ai Khanum contain posthumous imitations of Eucratides and Heliocles. New rulers reused familiar Greek royal designs instead of inventing money from nothing. The coins reveal continuity in workshops and exchange, though a copied portrait does not identify the ethnicity of every maker or user.

More than a century after the migration, Kujula Kadphises of Guishuang overcame the other chiefs and styled himself king. His coins gradually replaced earlier names and adopted larger titles. This was the political formation of Kushan rule, usually placed around 30 CE, not an event in 100 BCE.

At Ai Khanum, handmade bottle-shaped pots have been proposed as Yuezhi and goblets on stands as Saka. Yet only a small quantity of “nomadic” ware appeared beside continuing Greco-Bactrian pottery, and scholars caution that exact ethnic labels remain hypothetical. A pot shape is evidence, not a passport.

Khalchayan in southern Uzbekistan preserves the clearest named Yuezhi-Kushan setting used here. Excavations from 1959 to 1963 uncovered a palace with painted, almost life-size clay figures. The palace is often dated to the mid-first century BCE, but its precise date and ruler remain disputed.

The Khalchayan palace was a one-story rectangle with a small aiwan portico, a throne room and corridors leading to surrounding rooms. Those walls turn “rule” into a built place where visitors, guards, attendants and elites moved, although the plan tells us little about ordinary tents or farmhouses.

Dalverzin Tepe grew from a small fortified place into an extensive walled town in the first century BCE and is proposed as a Yuezhi capital. Its best-described administrative, residential, religious and manufacturing zones belong mainly to the later Kushan city. The identification is useful, but not certain enough to redraw the atlas.

At first-century CE Tillya Tepe, archaeologists found a nomadic chieftain and women buried with thousands of gold objects. The cemetery belongs to the region’s post-migration nomadic world, but the museum does not securely call its occupants Yuezhi. It is comparative evidence, not a family photograph of this atlas label.

Khalchayan’s throne-hall sculptures show rulers and aristocrats under deities drawn from Iranian, West Asian and Hellenistic traditions. One surviving head may represent an ancestor. These are elite claims about protection and legitimacy, carefully staged in a palace, not a complete list of what every household believed.

The battle, hunting and enthronement scenes at Khalchayan used Hellenized sculptural methods for Iranian and Central Asian themes. That combination is an achievement of adaptation: artists learned an inherited technique, changed its subjects and made a visual language for new rulers instead of merely copying Greek art.

Other Khalchayan walls showed festivals and religious ceremonies with musicians, masked performers and comedians. A palace image cannot prove how often ordinary people attended or performed, but it is vivid evidence that elite public culture included music, costume and laughter as well as battle scenes.

Tillya Tepe jewelry mixes steppe animals, Greek cupids, Indian motifs and Chinese-looking dragons. Goldsmiths did not live inside sealed cultural boxes. Because these graves date to the first century CE and their occupants are not securely identified, the objects illuminate a connected Bactrian world rather than a uniquely Yuezhi style.

Later Kushan coins show Iranian, Hindu and Buddhist divine figures and royal clothing beside inherited Greek forms. Scholars read this broad pantheon as a strategy for ruling culturally different regions. It demonstrates political creativity by the successor empire, while remaining too late to define Yuezhi belief in 200 BCE.

The Shiji says the Xiongnu killed a Yuezhi king and the people later established his heir. That single royal succession proves that a dynasty mattered at one crisis. It does not reveal a complete inheritance law, the authority of ordinary parents or a general gender system for Yuezhi families.

At Khalchayan, a king and queen sit among Bactrian and Parthian princes and warrior nobles. The arrangement displays rank, dynasty and alliance. It tells us that elite family relationships mattered to royal imagery, but says nothing reliable about the household size, marriage rules or authority of ordinary families.

Tillya Tepe placed a male chieftain at the mound’s highest central point and female graves around him. Different goods may mark status, but the women’s relationship to him and their causes of death are uncertain. The cemetery cannot supply a universal Yuezhi family tree.

No schoolroom, primer or Yuezhi child’s exercise securely appears in the sources reviewed for this card. Later coins and multilingual inscriptions prove that some specialists learned scripts, formulas and die-cutting. They do not reveal where children studied, who taught them or how widely literacy reached.

Khalchayan’s artists mastered modeling, paint, large compositions and several visual traditions. Those skills had to be learned through practice, but no named teacher or apprentice survives. “Workshop learning” is a cautious inference from skilled production, not evidence for a formal academy run by Yuezhi rulers.

Zhang Qian described the Great Yuezhi as moving with their herds and changing camps. That supports pastoral mobility, but his short report does not list species, recipes, milking, meal times or who cooked. A child-friendly story still has to stop where the menu disappears from the evidence.

Bactria was different from an empty pasture. Economic history contrasts the mobile Yuezhi with settled agricultural regions, then follows later Kushan canals, markets and workshops. Political conquest changed who received obedience without instantly turning every farmer or craft worker into a nomad.

Later Kushan-period excavations found millet, barley, wheat, fruits, grapes, melons, sesame, fodder and cotton. These finds show what the broader region could grow and make after Yuezhi settlement. They are not a grocery receipt for the migrating confederation, and direct early Yuezhi food remains stay sparse.

Elite figures at Khalchayan wear belted mantles over shirts, long trousers or leggings, boots and shoulder cloths. Women are shown in layered floor-length dresses, shoes and tiaras or crowns. Sculpture preserves dress choices, but court art should not become a uniform for every child, herder or farmer.

Tiny gold and turquoise plaques from Tillya Tepe were sewn onto hats and robes. Turquoise, carnelian and amethyst point toward several supply regions, and wear on objects shows some were used before burial. These dazzling clothes belonged to a later nomadic elite, not everyone living under Yuezhi rule.

sections.title: Health, water and the toilet question

items.text: Direct evidence for a Yuezhi physician, remedy or medical school has not been established in the sources reviewed here. A later Kushan inscription connects a dedication with a wish for a king’s health, but records no diagnosis or treatment. Anything more specific would be invention, not medicine history.

The museum account says no evidence shows how the Tillya Tepe people died. Sickness, environment and sacrifice have all been suggested, but none is demonstrated. This is a useful lesson in archaeological restraint: rich graves can preserve jewelry brilliantly while preserving a life story very poorly.

Bactrian farming depended on water long before and after the migration. In the Kushan era, canal irrigation and animal-drawn ploughs expanded. That later infrastructure shows rulers and communities managing an arid landscape, but it cannot prove that a named Yuezhi inventor designed each canal or farming tool.

At the later Kushan sanctuary of Surkh Kotal, an inscription and excavated works record a failed water supply followed by a lined well and assigned caretakers. It is unusually concrete evidence for maintenance and clean water in the successor state, many generations after the atlas’s 200 to 100 BCE window.

Published descriptions of Khalchayan’s portico, throne hall, corridors and surrounding rooms do not identify a latrine, sewer or toilet. That means this card cannot tell children what a Yuezhi toilet looked like. It does not prove that people lacked waste practices; the direct evidence is simply sparse.

The names Yuezhi and Great Yuezhi reach us through Chinese writing, not through a surviving self-description in a Yuezhi language. Later Kushan rulers used several regional languages and scripts. None proves the language spoken by every family during the migration from Gansu to Bactria.

An authentic successor-period sample, in the published diplomatic capitals, is OOHMO KAΔΦIΣHΣO ϷAO, read “Vima Kadphises the king.” It represents Bactrian in Greek-derived script and survives in the Rabatak genealogy, composed after about 132 CE. It is Kushan royal writing, not a Yuezhi sentence from 200 BCE.

Kushan coins made writing portable. A British Museum coin of Kanishka bears a Bactrian inscription, while earlier rulers had used Greek legends and inherited designs. Coins joined portrait, title, deity and metal in a tiny political message that could travel far beyond a palace wall.

Zhang Qian’s Yuezhi mission helped begin recorded direct contact between Han China and Iranian lands near the end of the second century BCE. The exchange network had older paths and many local middlemen. It is clearer to say the mission expanded official knowledge than to claim one traveler “invented” the Silk Road.

Yuezhi political organization became part of a Kushan state that blended local Bactrian, Hellenistic, Indian and nomadic practices. Later empires and dynasties changed again. The old label faded, but towns, farms, families, craft knowledge, languages and memories continued through every shift in royal name.

ending.text: The Yuezhi did not disappear when the atlas id stops at 100 BCE. Its instant Kushan successor polygon is chronologically premature. Historical accounts instead place several Yuezhi domains in Bactria and say that, more than a century after the migration, Kujula Kadphises of the Kushan branch overcame the other chiefs and called himself king, usually placed around 30 CE. That transformation ended a separate Yuezhi political arrangement, not its communities. Kushan rulers adopted Bactrian and other regional institutions, expanded south and built a diverse empire. Later Kushan fragmentation ended particular courts; descendants, subjects, towns, farming and artistic traditions continued under changing powers.
